title: Jamie Dimon Just Said 5 Words Blocking Outside AI Agents From JPMorgan Accounts: "You Don't Want Rogue Agents." Here's Why That Security Stance Matters for JPM and Its Tech Rivals. - The Globe and Mail
content: Personal AI agents like Meta’s Muse can help people offload everyday tasks and manage their money with an AI helper -- but not every bank is interested in allowing access. On last month’s earnings call, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warned against the risk of “rogue agents” and said that his bank would not allow “just any” outside AI agents. United Airlines just announced a similar move to block access to third-party AI agents used for booking flights. Agentic AI is often described as the next wave of artificial intelligence (AI) technology. With AI agents, people can use AI to automate various tasks for them, at work and in their personal lives. A prominent recent example is Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META), which made a big splash in September with the launch of Muse, its personal AI agent. Meta's Muse is designed to help people offload some of their everyday online tasks, like sending emails, filling out forms, booking travel, and even shopping. It reached the rare milestone of 10 million downloads after only 40 days on the market and was widely praised for its ease of use and making agentic AI "real" for consumers. If users give permission and access to their banking and credit card data, Muse can even help people with financial tasks and managing money, like setting a budget, negotiating bills, or canceling unwanted subscriptions. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » But what if banks don't allow Muse (or other AI agents) to connect to their customers' accounts? There are cybersecurity and liability questions involved with allowing people to use AI agents for sensitive financial tasks like managing a bank account, trading stocks, or making credit card payments. Not every bank is on board with this. Last month on the bank's quarterly earnings call, Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), sounded a five-word warning about the future of AI agents for banking. He said, "You don't want rogue agents." Let's look at what Dimon's remarks might mean for AI agents -- and why JPMorgan Chase is not the only company figuring out how to accept outside AI agents. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. Image source: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Banks must follow strict regulations called "Know Your Customer" rules. That means banks are required to know who is accessing an account, who is authorizing a transaction, and other details to identify customers to help prevent financial fraud and money laundering. AI agents could potentially bring complexity and added risk to banks' "Know Your Customer" compliance. What if an AI agent "goes rogue" and makes an unauthorized transaction, or is used to commit financial crimes? What if an AI agent gets into a part of the customer's account that the customer didn't allow? What if a customer later claims that a purchase was fraudulent, even though the customer allowed their AI agent to execute the transaction? Most banks would rather not deal with these hassles and extra risks. Allowing third-party agents like Meta Muse might create liabilities for banks and their customers that banks can't control and didn't choose. On the October earnings call, Jamie Dimon also said that at JPMorgan Chase, "we are not gonna allow just any agent to come, outside agent to come inside the company because it is just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan." On Wednesday, United Airlines(NASDAQ: UAL) announced that it is restricting access for unauthorized third-party AI agents or assistants. The airline's statement referred to the risks of AI agents causing unauthorized bookings, unintended usage of airline frequent flyer miles, and possible violations of FAA and DOT safety regulations for airline passengers. United Airlines is another example of a business in a heavily regulated industry that must manage sensitive transactions and confidential customer data. And they're tapping the brakes on AI agents. If other banks and airlines adopt this same security-oriented stance, the future of personal agentic AI for companies like Meta Platforms might become less user-friendly -- and less profitable. title: JPMorgan Stock Slid After Reports That Senate Democrats Plan a New Investigation Into Jamie Dimon's Bank Over Its Jeffrey Epstein Relationship. Here's Why That Political Risk Could Weigh on JPM Shares. - The Motley Fool
content: JPMorgan Chase and CEO Jamie Dimon have been scrutinized over their relationship with disgraced sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, who died in 2019. The Democrats will control Congress starting in early 2027, which likely means more regulatory scrutiny of the financial sector, although the regulatory agencies will still be led by Trump administration appointees. JPMorgan Chase (JPM +0.98%), the largest bank in the country, got its first dose of this when CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee plan to further investigate the bank's ties to the late Jeffrey Epstein, who was arrested in 2019 for the sex trafficking of minors before his subsequent death. JPMorgan's stock fell that day on these reports. Here's why this political risk could weigh on shares. Epstein had a 15-year banking relationship with JPMorgan Chase between 1998 and 2013. U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), in a letter to the bank, claimed Epstein opened 134 accounts at the bank, which processed over $1 billion in transactions for Epstein. In 2003, JPMorgan reportedly generated $8 million in fees from Epstein, wrote Warren. Former longtime executive Jes Staley, who worked at JPMorgan for three decades and led several of the bank's divisions, reportedly exchanged over 1,200 emails with Epstein between 2008 and 2012, became friendly with him, and defended him, despite what a Congressional committee chair described as "red flags." In 2008, Epstein pleaded guilty to soliciting prostitution and procuring a person under the age of 18 for prostitution. Staley left JPMorgan in 2013 and eventually became the CEO of Barclays, a British bank. However, Staley stepped down from this role in 2021 after British regulators found that he had mischaracterized his dealings with Epstein. In 2023, a class action lawsuit involving 200 victims of Epstein targeted JPMorgan Chase for its role in Epstein's crimes and secured a $290 million settlement (along with $75 million paid to the U.S. Virgin Islands, though no admission of wrongdoing came with the settlement). JPMorgan's current CEO, Jamie Dimon, who took over the bank in 2006, said in 2023, "I am so sad that we had any relationship to that man whatsoever." However, the bank’sDimon had no "specific knowledge" of Epstein. Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR), who is expected to take over the Senate Finance Committee in 2027, said in a statement that all financial players who played a role in facilitating Epstein's crimes "... will be forced to answer to the Senate Finance Committee for their role in hurting the American people and enabling Trump's corruption." A JPMorgan spokesperson said the government had damning information it never shared with the bank, and that the bank regrets the association but didn’t help Epstein commit his crimes. Congressional committees do not have the authority to impose fines or regulatory orders on banks. However, they can conduct investigations that can compel executives to testify before Congress through subpoenas, and then refer their findings to regulatory agencies or other departments that do have the authority to issue punitive orders. If the Senate Finance Committee or another committee were to find further wrongdoing by the bank, it could still lead to another fine or regulatory order requiring JPMorgan Chase to boost compliance efforts, including monitoring transactions for fraud and conducting background checks on ultra-high-net-worth clients. This could lead to higher-than-expected expenses, which would hurt the stock. If Dimon is found to have known more than he let on, perhaps he would be removed as CEO, which would materially impact the stock. Dimon is one of the most respected CEOs on Wall Street, so if he is no longer running the bank, the stock may struggle for a period as investors adjust to a new leader, although I view Dimon's removal as unlikely right now. Finally, putting JPMorgan Chase and its relationship with Epstein further under the spotlight could lead to reputational damage, which is important in any sector. Some might argue that large banks like JPMorgan Chase are still dealing with reputational damage from the 2008 Great Recession. Ultimately, while it's impossible to predict what could come to light in a new investigation, if there even is one, I am not overly concerned about JPMorgan Chase's long-term prospects, as I don't think any new findings will ultimately harm the core business. They could, however, lead to a near-term drawdown in shares or weigh on the stock until the findings of such an investigation are made clear. title: J.P. Morgan’s $55 Target Says IREN’s Selloff Went Too Far - TIKR.com
content: @Ali Raza via Canva, @Brett Sayles from Pexels via Canva IREN (IREN) has fallen approximately 71% from its May 27 closing high of $67.84 as investors reassess the company’s ambitious AI infrastructure expansion. J.P. Morgan analyst Richard Choe lowered the firm’s price target from $65 to $55 on November 9 while maintaining an Overweight rating. Selling pressure intensified after reports that Microsoft was increasing oversight of third-party data center projects amid concerns about construction delays and infrastructure delivery. During its November 5 fiscal first-quarter earnings announcement, IREN pushed its target of more than $4 billion in contracted annual recurring revenue from year-end 2026 to January 2027, with a possible extension into February. Co-CEO Daniel Roberts attributed the revised timeline to customer-requested changes and supplier timing, explaining that the milestone “may extend to the end of February.” Despite the delay, IREN reported a 182% sequential increase in AI Cloud revenue to $200 million, while contracted revenue backlog rose 22% to $20.3 billion, according to its fiscal first-quarter earnings release. These results suggest substantial contracted demand, but investors remain concerned about how quickly IREN can bring additional capacity online and translate that demand into recognized revenue. IREN appears potentially undervalued if its delayed infrastructure projects become operational and its fiscal 2028 growth expectations remain achievable. According to TIKR estimates dated November 9, analysts projected $2.39 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, down from $2.81 billion in late October.
